steps.title: Names, passwords, sentences
steps.body:
Half of all placement coding questions involve text: palindromes, vowels, reversing words, checking a password. In Java, text is a `String`, a row of characters with **positions** just like an array.

In five minutes you’ll pull a string apart, meet the comparison bug that fails real interviews, and reverse a word yourself.

options.why: length() counts characters (4). It’s the last INDEX that is 3.
Right: charAt(0) is J, upper is JAVA, and length() is 4.
upper holds the new uppercase string, and that is what gets printed.
Positions start at 0, so charAt(0) is the first character, J.

steps.title: The string toolkit
points: `s.length()`, `s.charAt(i)`, `s.substring(a, b)` (from a up to, but **not including**, b), `s.indexOf("x")`.
Strings are **immutable**: `toUpperCase()`, `replace()` and friends return a *new* string.
Compare text with `a.equals(b)`, **never** `a == b`. `==` checks whether they are the same object.
Loop over characters with `for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++)` and `s.charAt(i)`.

steps.prompt: A classic trap. What does this print?

options.why: equals compares the characters, and "code" equals "code".
Yes. equals compares the text (same), while == compares the objects (different).
== asks "same object?", and new String made a different object with the same text. Use equals for text.
It’s the other way round: equals looks at the text.

steps.prompt: Your turn. Build the word backwards, one character at a time.
steps.hint: The loop walks i from the last index down to 0. Add the character at position i.
steps.explain: `word.charAt(i)` adds each character from the end first, so "stressed" becomes "desserts".
